lessons.title: Why Breakouts Fail So Often
lessons.summary: Explain what actually happens in the order book when a level breaks, and use it to predict which breakouts are likely to fail before you risk a penny.
lessons.module_title: Module 1 — Why Breaks Fail, and Where They Start
lessons.html:
Every trader has bought a breakout at the exact high of the day. The level snaps, a big green candle surges through, you buy — and within three candles price is back inside the range, your stop is gone, and the market is running hard the other way. It feels personal. It is not. It is mechanical, and once you understand the mechanism, you stop being its fuel.

This course is about trading breakouts properly: which ones to take, which ones to leave, and why the most reliable entry usually comes after the break, when price returns to test the level it just broke. But we start with failure, because failure is the normal state of affairs. If you take one idea from this first lesson, take this: a breakout is not a signal. It is a question the market asks, and most of the time the answer is no.

Markets breathe in, then out

Markets do not trend all the time. Most of the time price drifts sideways in a band while buyers and sellers agree, roughly, on what something is worth. Candles are small. Swings are short. Then, occasionally, the agreement breaks down — news lands, positions get too crowded, a big order arrives — and price moves fast and far until it finds a new area of agreement.

That alternation — contraction, then expansion — is the reason breakout trading exists. Contraction stores energy: positions build up on both sides of a range, and so do the stop-losses protecting them. Expansion releases it. The breakout trader's job is to be positioned for the release without being fooled by the many false starts that precede it.

Where the orders actually sit

To understand why breaks fail, you need a picture of what is resting around an obvious range. There are three clusters of orders, and none of them are secret.

Stop-losses. Traders who sold the range high have protective buy stops just above it. Traders who bought the range low have sell stops just beneath it.

Breakout entries. Traders waiting for the level to go have buy-stop orders above resistance and sell-stop orders below support.

Range traders. People who intend to keep selling the top and buying the bottom until proven wrong, plus those taking profit from earlier moves.

When price pushes through the range high, the first two clusters fire together. Shorts are forced to buy back; breakout traders buy to enter. That is a burst of one-way demand hitting a patch of the order book where sellers have been filled or have stepped away. Price jumps. This is why genuine breakouts often move quickly: they are partly powered by traders who are wrong and have to exit, which is the most motivated buying in the market.

Now notice the problem. That burst is finite. Once the trapped shorts have covered and the eager breakout buyers are filled, the move needs a second wave — fresh buyers who want to own the market at higher prices — or it stalls. And if a large seller was waiting for exactly this burst of buying to sell into, the burst is the end of the move, not the start.

The trap, step by step

Large participants cannot fill big orders in a quiet market; they need someone on the other side. The pool of buy orders above an obvious range high is the most convenient place on the chart to sell size, because thousands of buy orders trigger there at once. So price spikes above the level, the buying is absorbed, and the market falls back through. Everyone who bought the break is now trapped above, and their stops — back inside the range — become fuel for the move down.

No conspiracy is required. Nobody needs to "hunt" anybody. Liquidity simply clusters where the crowd puts its orders, and large orders go where the liquidity is.

Look at the sequence carefully, because you will see it hundreds of times. The break looked convincing; it even closed above the level. The next candle handed it all back. Within a dozen bars price had travelled the full height of the range and broken the other side. Failed breakouts very often produce fast journeys to the opposite boundary, because the trapped traders have to get out and their exits all point the same way.

KEY POINT

A breakout is powered partly by traders who are forced to exit. That fuel runs out. If no fresh buyers arrive to replace it, the break fails — and the breakout buyers become the next forced exit.

What a break the market accepts looks like

Compare that with a break the market actually wants. The difference is rarely in the breakout candle itself. It is in what happens over the next few candles.

Three things separate this from the trap. First, the approach: lows were rising into the ceiling, so buyers were already turning up earlier each time. Second, the close: a full-bodied candle that finished well beyond the zone, not a wick poking through it. Third, acceptance: price paused but lived comfortably above the old resistance instead of slicing back through it. You will learn to grade all three in Module 2.

Breaks fail for reasons you can see in advance

Most failed breakouts are not random. They carry fingerprints that are visible before the trade. The common ones:

  • No compression. The "range" was sloppy and overlapping, with spikes out of both sides. Nothing was coiled, so nothing was stored.
  • A bigger wall just beyond. The level broke straight into a higher-timeframe level a few dozen pips away. There was no room to run.
  • Against the higher-timeframe trend. A break against the dominant flow needs much stronger evidence, because the larger players are positioned the other way.
  • The wrong hour. Thin, late-session or holiday conditions. A breakout needs participation. No participants, no breakout — just a spike.
  • A wick, not a close. Price traded beyond the level but the candle closed back inside. That is a rejection dressed as a breakout.

This last chart is the most painful kind of failure, because the break itself was textbook. Strong candle, clean close, obvious level. The trader did everything right at the level and nothing right around it. A daily resistance level sat just 26 pips overhead; the target required price to travel through it. The break ran straight into the wall and died.

COMMON MISTAKE

Judging a breakout only by the breakout candle. The candle tells you about the next hour. The level map tells you whether the next hour has anywhere to go.

Two ways to lose with breakouts

Breakout traders lose money in two distinct ways, and the second is sneakier than the first.

The first is obvious: chasing traps. You see a surging candle, fear missing out, and buy at the worst possible price — the exact place the pool of buy orders is being sold into. Then you hold a losing position on the wrong side of a failed level.

The second is the whipsaw of conviction. After being trapped three times, you refuse the next break — and that one is genuine and runs for two days without you. Burned out of money, then burned out of confidence. Most breakout traders cycle between these two states, letting the last trade decide how they treat the next one.

The way out is not courage. It is a written process: which levels, which conditions, which candle, which entry and which invalidation, decided before the session starts. Then the surging candle is just data against a checklist rather than a starting gun. That process is what this course builds, piece by piece.

Going deeper

For experienced traders, it is worth being precise about what "fail" means, because your testing depends on it. Three definitions are common, and they produce very different numbers:

  1. Close-back-inside failure — the break is dead the moment a candle on your timeframe closes back inside the range. Strict, fast, and the definition this course uses for exits.
  2. Opposite-side failure — the break is only counted as failed if price reaches the far side of the range. More forgiving, and it inflates apparent success.
  3. R-based failure — the trade hits a fixed stop before a fixed target. This is the only definition that tells you about expectancy, because it includes your actual entry and exit rules.

Public estimates of breakout failure rates vary enormously because definitions vary, and because failure depends heavily on market, timeframe and session. We will not quote a number. Measure your own, on your own definition, on at least a hundred historical examples, and track trend-aligned and counter-trend breaks separately — they behave differently.

There is also a structural reason breakouts appear to fail more than they succeed: the denominator. Price touches and briefly exceeds levels constantly, and every one of those touches looks like a potential breakout in real time. Only a minority become sustained expansions. This is not a flaw in the strategy; it is the base rate the strategy has to filter. The edge, if there is one, comes from discarding most breaks and paying a good price for the few that pass.

Finally, an expectancy point, with clearly hypothetical numbers. Suppose a filtered breakout approach wins only 40% of the time but its winners average 2R and its losers 1R. Its expectancy is (0.4 × 2) − (0.6 × 1) = +0.2R per trade before costs. A strategy can be right less than half the time and still have a positive expectation — but only if its losses are kept small and cut quickly, which is exactly what breakout traders find hardest when a trap closes around them.

THE RULES
  • A breakout is a question, not a signal. Never enter on the break alone without your other conditions.
  • Only a candle close beyond the level counts as a break. A wick beyond the level is a rejection.
  • Check the level map beyond the break before entry: no room to run, no trade.
  • A close back inside the range ends the breakout idea immediately. Exit without negotiation.

Summary

  • Markets alternate between contraction and expansion. Breakouts are the moment stored energy is released — or appears to be.
  • Above an obvious range high sit shorts' stops and breakout buy orders; that pool of buying is what powers breaks and what larger sellers sell into.
  • Failed breaks often run quickly to the other side of the range, because the trapped breakout buyers must exit.
  • Genuine breaks are usually built (compression, rising lows), closed decisively, and accepted on the far side.
  • Many failures are predictable: sloppy ranges, a bigger level just beyond, counter-trend breaks, dead sessions and wick-only breaks.

quiz.q: Why do genuine upside breakouts often move quickly at first?
options: Brokers widen spreads after a break
Short sellers' stops and breakout buy orders trigger together, creating a burst of one-way buying
Range traders always buy the break
Central banks intervene at round numbers
quiz.why: Forced short covering plus fresh breakout entries create concentrated buying in a thin part of the order book. The other options are not the mechanism.

quiz.q: In the 'trap' chart, what was the decisive evidence that the breakout had failed?
options: The breakout candle had a large body
The next candle closed back inside the range
Price later broke the range low
The range had four touches
quiz.why: A close back inside the range ends the breakout idea. Breaking the range low happened later — by then the damage to breakout buyers was done.

quiz.q: A strong H1 breakout candle closes above a range, but a daily resistance level sits 20 pips above. What is the main problem?
options: The candle is too strong
There is no room to run before a bigger level
H1 breakouts never work
The range was too long
quiz.why: The break itself can be perfect and still fail because it runs straight into a higher-timeframe wall. Check the map beyond the level before entry.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a common fingerprint of a breakout likely to fail?
options: A sloppy, overlapping range with spikes on both sides
A break during thin, late-session conditions
Rising lows pressing into a flat ceiling before the break
A wick through the level with a close back inside
quiz.why: Rising lows into a ceiling show buyers arriving earlier — a sign of a built, healthier break. The other three are classic failure warnings.

quiz.q: Hypothetically, a strategy wins 40% of trades, with winners averaging 2R and losers 1R. What is its expectancy before costs?
options: 0R
quiz.why: (0.4 × 2) − (0.6 × 1) = 0.8 − 0.6 = +0.2R. A lower win rate can still be positive if losses stay small — the numbers here are illustrative only.

quiz.q: What is the 'whipsaw of conviction'?
options: Price breaking both sides of a range in one session
Refusing a genuine breakout because recent traps have shaken your confidence
Moving your stop to breakeven too early
Trading two breakouts at once
quiz.why: After repeated traps, traders often skip the next valid break. A written process stops the last trade from deciding how you treat the next one.

lessons.title: Compression and Volatility Squeezes
lessons.summary: Recognise a market that is genuinely coiling before a break, measure the squeeze objectively, and reject sideways noise that only looks like a consolidation.
lessons.module_title: Module 1 — Why Breaks Fail, and Where They Start
lessons.html:
The best breakouts are loaded long before they fire. Hours or days before the big candle, the market goes quiet: candles shrink, swings get shorter, and price presses into a smaller and smaller box. Most traders find this phase boring and either ignore it or trade inside it out of restlessness. Breakout traders should find it the most interesting part of the chart, because it tells you where the energy is being stored and roughly when it is likely to be released.

This lesson teaches you to see compression, to measure it without guesswork, and — just as important — to tell a genuine coil from a sideways mess that will only produce false breaks.

Volatility moves in cycles

Volatility is not constant. It contracts and expands in a rough cycle: a period of large candles and wide swings is usually followed by a period of small candles and narrow swings, and that quiet period is usually followed by expansion again. It is one of the more dependable behaviours in markets, and it is the backbone of breakout trading.

Why does it happen? During a quiet phase, buyers and sellers agree on value, so price can move only a little before it meets an order on the other side. Positions build up on both sides and so do their stop-losses, packed into a narrower band. When price finally escapes, it does so through a crowd of stops all clustered close together — which is why quiet periods so often end with a fast move.

Three ways to see a squeeze

You do not need an indicator to see compression, but you do need to look for it deliberately. Three measures, from simplest to most precise:

1. Candle size. Compare the last ten candles with the twenty before them. In a squeeze, bodies and wicks shrink visibly. If you need to squint to decide whether candles are smaller, they probably are not.

2. Swing size. Measure each swing inside the consolidation — high to low, low to high. In a coil, each swing is shorter than the one before. Lower highs and higher lows, or a flat side with the other side closing in.

3. Band width. Bollinger Bands (20-period, 2 standard deviations) widen when volatility rises and narrow when it falls. When the bands are at their narrowest for the last 50–100 bars, you have an objective squeeze. Average True Range (ATR) does a similar job as a single number.

KEY POINT

A squeeze tells you that a move is coming and roughly when. It does not tell you which way. Direction comes from the break itself — and from the lean of the structure and the higher-timeframe trend.

What makes a consolidation tradeable

Not every sideways period is a coil. Your filter should be strict, because the quality of the consolidation is one of the strongest predictors of the quality of the break. A tradeable consolidation has four features:

Defined boundaries. At least two clean touches on each side, so you know exactly what a break would mean. Three on the side you plan to trade through is better.

Meaningful duration. Long enough, relative to your timeframe, for positions to build. On an H1 chart, think a day or more of sideways price — roughly 20 bars or longer — not ninety minutes of lunchtime drift.

Contraction. Swings shrinking, candles shrinking, or price pressing repeatedly against one side. A consolidation where volatility is rising is not loading energy; it is spending it.

Context. A pause inside a trend is a continuation candidate. A consolidation that formed after a long trend, at a major higher-timeframe level, may be a turning point instead. Neither is wrong, but they are different trades.

The lean: which side is losing patience?

Compression often has a shape, and the shape tells you which side is losing the argument. When lows rise into a flat ceiling, buyers are stepping in earlier and higher each time while sellers merely defend a fixed price. Each test of the ceiling eats a little more of the resting supply. That is a bullish lean. The mirror image — lower highs pressing into a flat floor — is a bearish lean.

A lean is a tilt, not a promise. It raises your standard for a break in the opposite direction and lowers your resistance to taking one in the same direction. Lesson 8 covers these shapes properly as triangles.

When sideways is just noise

Here is what most sideways price actually looks like, and why you should leave it alone.

The chart has no consistent boundaries, swings are not shrinking, and spikes pierce both sides every few hours. Breaks from structures like this are much more likely to fail, because there is no crowd neatly positioned at a clear level and no stored energy behind the move. Every "breakout" is just the next swing.

COMMON MISTAKE

Drawing a range around any sideways price and treating every exit from it as a breakout. If the boundaries keep moving, the range does not exist.

The squeeze does not tell you the direction

The final piece is humility about direction. A squeeze inside an uptrend is more likely to resolve upward, but it does not have to. When it breaks against the trend, believe the break that happened, not the one you expected.

Notice too that the downside break did not come out of nowhere. The squeeze had sat above the 50 EMA for a long time without making progress, and the floor of the box was the obvious place for longs to have their stops. When it went, those stops became sellers. The same mechanics from Lesson 1 apply in either direction.

This is why the plan is never "buy the squeeze". The plan is "the squeeze is loading; mark both boundaries; wait for a candle to close through one of them; then judge that break on its own merits". You may decide in advance that you will only trade upside breaks in an uptrend — a perfectly sensible filter — but you must still respect a downside break as information: the uptrend thesis has just been damaged.

Going deeper

Making the squeeze objective. For systematic testing you need a rule, not an impression. Two common definitions, both of which you should test rather than trust:

  • Bandwidth percentile: Bollinger bandwidth = (upper band − lower band) ÷ middle band. Flag a squeeze when the current bandwidth is in the lowest 10–20% of its last 100–120 readings.
  • ATR ratio: compare a short ATR (say 10 bars) with a long ATR (say 50 bars). A ratio below roughly 0.6–0.7 marks a quiet regime. These thresholds are starting points for your own testing, not magic numbers.

The head fake. A well-known squeeze behaviour is the initial move out of the bands that quickly reverses and is followed by the real expansion in the opposite direction. It is the false break of Lesson 7 viewed through volatility: the first push collects the stops on one side, then the market goes the other way. This is one of the strongest arguments for the retest entry — a head fake rarely offers a clean, holding retest.

Nested compression. The most powerful squeezes often appear on two timeframes at once: a daily inside bar or narrow-range day, inside which the H1 chart shows a tight range. When the H1 range breaks, it is also breaking the daily structure, and both groups of traders are acting at once. Check the timeframe above yours whenever you find a good coil.

Squeeze length and decay. Compression does not store energy for ever. A consolidation that drags on far longer than normal for that market often leaks its energy: participants lose interest, stops get moved and the eventual break is a dribble. Long is good; endless is not. In triangles this shows up as the apex deadline, covered in Lesson 8.

Session effects. Many FX squeezes are simply the Asian session. The overnight range on EUR/USD or GBP/USD is often tight because the main participants are not yet active; it is not compression in the energy-storing sense. Breaks of the Asian range at the London open are a separate, well-known setup with its own failure patterns — treat them as such rather than as evidence of a multi-day coil.

THE RULES
  • Do not trade inside a squeeze. The trade is the resolution, not the coil.
  • Require at least two touches on each boundary and visible contraction before calling it a consolidation.
  • A squeeze gives timing, not direction. Wait for a candle to close through one side.
  • If the swings are not shrinking and the boundaries keep moving, it is noise — skip it.

Summary

  • Volatility contracts and expands in cycles; quiet phases pack positions and stops into a narrow band.
  • Measure compression three ways: shrinking candles, shrinking swings, and narrowing Bollinger bandwidth or ATR.
  • A tradeable consolidation has defined boundaries, enough duration, contraction and clear context.
  • Shape gives a lean (rising lows into a flat top is bullish), but a squeeze never guarantees direction.
  • Sideways noise with moving boundaries is not a coil and produces unreliable breaks.

quiz.q: What does a volatility squeeze tell you most reliably?
options: The direction of the next move
That a larger move is becoming more likely, not which way
The exact target of the breakout
That the trend will continue
quiz.why: Compression signals stored energy and rough timing. Direction comes from the break itself, as the gold chart showed.

quiz.q: On an H1 chart, which consolidation best meets this course's definition of tradeable?
options: 90 minutes of sideways drift at lunchtime
Two days with 3 touches at the top, 2 at the bottom, and shrinking swings
A week of wide swings with spikes through both sides
One touch of resistance followed by a dip
quiz.why: Defined boundaries, meaningful duration and contraction are all present. The others lack duration, contraction or boundaries.

quiz.q: In 'A coil: every swing smaller than the last', what made the structure a coil?
options: The candles were all green
Lower highs and higher lows squeezed each swing into less space
Price stayed above a moving average
The range was exactly 50 pips wide
quiz.why: Converging highs and lows — each swing shorter than the last — is the visual signature of compression.

quiz.q: Lows keep rising into a flat ceiling. What does that suggest?
options: Sellers are getting more aggressive
A bullish lean: buyers are stepping in earlier while sellers defend a fixed price
A guaranteed upside break
The range is about to widen
quiz.why: Rising lows show buyers' impatience. It is a lean, not a guarantee — downside breaks still happen.

quiz.q: What is a 'head fake' in squeeze trading?
options: A breakout candle with no wick
A first move out of the squeeze that reverses, followed by expansion the other way
A squeeze that lasts more than a week
A retest that holds perfectly
quiz.why: The initial push collects stops on one side and fails; the real expansion follows in the opposite direction. The retest entry helps filter it.

quiz.q: Why might the Asian session range on EUR/USD not count as a true multi-day squeeze?
options: Asian ranges are always too wide
The quiet is often just low participation, not stored energy from a multi-day contest
Asian session breaks never work
Bollinger Bands do not work at night
quiz.why: A narrow overnight range usually reflects absent participants rather than days of positions building — it is a different setup with its own behaviour.

lessons.title: Identifying the Level That Matters
lessons.summary: Build a clean level map in minutes, pick out the one level whose break is worth trading, and treat it as a zone rather than a laser line.
lessons.module_title: Module 1 — Why Breaks Fail, and Where They Start
lessons.html:
You can draw a horizontal line anywhere on a chart and price will eventually cross it. That does not make it a breakout. Before you think about candles, entries or stops, you need to answer one question: is this a level the market actually cares about, or a line I drew because I wanted a trade?

A breakout only travels if other people's orders are waiting beyond the level — stops, breakout entries, latecomers piling in. That only happens at levels the crowd can see. This lesson gives you a quick, repeatable way to find those levels and ignore the rest.

Three qualities of a level worth trading

1. It is obvious. This sounds backwards — surely the edge is in seeing what others miss? Not for breakouts. A breakout needs the crowd. If you needed a custom indicator and a squint to find a level, nobody's stops are there and nothing will happen when it breaks. Use the five-second test: show the chart to another trader and they should mark the same line within five seconds.

2. It is tested. A boundary that has rejected price three or four times means more than one touched once. Each rejection proves real orders defended it — and each one adds another batch of positions, and their stops, around it. More touches, more fuel when it finally gives way.

3. It is recent and relevant to your timeframe. If you trade the H1 chart, your working levels are the last few days to few weeks of structure: the current range, yesterday's high and low, this week's high and low, and recent swing points. Mark the big higher-timeframe levels too, because they explain why price sometimes stops dead in apparently open space — but trade the structure your timeframe respects.

Too many lines

Most traders' charts fail the first quality because they carry too many lines.

On this chart every candle touches something, so the lines carry no information. Worse, they give you a ready-made excuse for any trade you feel like taking. Five or six lines per pair, across all timeframes, is usually plenty.

Now the same price action carries a story: a ceiling rejected five times, lows rising into it. There is one level worth planning around, and you already know what a break of it would mean.

KEY POINT

The level that matters is the one the crowd can see, that has been defended repeatedly, and that sits on your timeframe's recent structure. Usually there is only one per chart.

Levels are zones, not laser lines

Forex prices differ slightly between brokers. Wicks overshoot. Orders cluster around a level rather than on a single pip. If you draw a level as a one-pip line, you will see "breaks" every time a wick pokes through by three pips, and you will miss genuine retests that dip a few pips into the area.

Draw the zone so it covers the cluster of closes and most of the wicks at the level. When you later ask "has this level broken?", the question becomes: has a candle closed clearly beyond the whole zone? That single habit removes a large share of false signals.

COMMON MISTAKE

Demanding pip-perfect precision. A wick three pips through a level is not a breakout, and a retest that dips three pips into the zone is not a failure.

Read how price arrived at the level

A level's history matters as much as its touch count. Ask three questions of any candidate level.

How did price leave it last time? A level that produced a sharp, fast rejection — big candles away from it — shows strong orders were waiting. A level price drifted away from lazily says less. The sharper the past reactions, the more stops are likely clustered beyond it, and the more violent the break when those orders are finally exhausted.

Has it switched sides before? A level that acted as resistance last month and support last week has been noticed by two different groups of traders. Levels with this kind of two-sided history tend to be watched closely, and they are often the levels where the retest — the subject of Lesson 6 — behaves best.

How is price approaching it now? Price grinding into a level with smaller and smaller pullbacks is pressure building against it. Price arriving in one vertical candle from the middle of nowhere has built nothing; it is as likely to bounce as to break. The approach is the first clue to the outcome, and you will grade it formally in Lesson 4.

These questions take seconds per level, and they do something useful for your psychology: they replace "will it break?" — which nobody can answer — with "what would a break here mean, and who would be caught by it?", which you can.

A two-minute level routine

Run this before each session, top down, so it becomes a checklist rather than an art project.

  1. Daily chart. Mark the major swing highs and lows of roughly the last three months, and any multi-day consolidation. These are context levels — the walls of the building.
  2. H4 chart. Where has price stalled repeatedly this week? Mark only levels with two or more clear reactions.
  3. Your execution timeframe (H1). Mark the current range if there is one, yesterday's high and low, and this week's high and low.
  4. Choose. Identify the one level whose break you would actually trade — the obvious, tested, recent one — and note the next higher-timeframe level beyond it. The distance between the two is your room to run.
  5. Delete. Remove any line price has spent a full session trading far beyond. Stale levels are clutter.

By way of illustration only: suppose GBP/USD has spent three days between 1.2620 and 1.2680, with three rejections at the top and two at the bottom, inside a daily uptrend, and the next daily resistance sits at 1.2790. The ceiling at 1.2680 is obvious, tested and recent; the daily trend leans upward; and there are 110 pips of room above it. You have not predicted anything. You have prepared.

The routine also protects you from the most expensive habit in breakout trading: discovering the level after the candle has broken it. A trader who spots a big green candle, scrolls left, and only then finds the level it broke is reacting, not planning. Everything about that trade — the entry, the stop, the target — is improvised under adrenaline. A trader who marked the level before the session already knows what a break would look like, where the stop would go and where the next wall sits. The break becomes a box to tick rather than a decision to make.

Practice drill

Going deeper

Which levels attract the most orders. In FX, a handful of reference levels draw disproportionate attention because so many participants use them: the previous day's high and low, the previous week's high and low, the Asian session range, recent swing extremes and round numbers such as 1.0900 or 150.00. A range boundary that coincides with one of these (a "stacked" level) tends to carry more resting orders. Note the stacking on your map.

Recency versus significance. There is a tension between a fresh H1 level and an old daily one. A practical rule: the higher-timeframe level wins on direction and targets, and the execution-timeframe level wins on timing and entry. You buy the H1 break; you take profit before the daily wall.

Touch counting has diminishing returns. Two touches define a level; three confirm it; a fifth or sixth touch often means the defending orders are being worn away. Repeated tests can make a break more likely, not less — which is one reason flat-topped structures with rising lows lean towards an upside resolution.

Measuring room to run in risk units. Before any breakout trade, estimate where your stop would sit and divide the distance to the next real level by that stop distance. If a 20-pip stop faces a daily level 25 pips away, the trade offers barely 1R before it hits a wall. Many traders set a minimum of 2R of clear space as a filter. Treat that figure as a starting point for your own testing, not a law.

THE RULES
  • Trade breaks only of levels that pass the five-second test and have at least two clear reactions.
  • Draw every level as a zone covering the cluster of closes and most of the wicks.
  • A break means a close clearly beyond the whole zone, not a wick through a line.
  • Note the next higher-timeframe level before every trade; skip breaks with less than about 2R of room.
  • Keep the map lean: five or six lines per pair, refreshed before each session.

Summary

  • A breakout needs the crowd's orders beyond the level, so the level must be obvious, tested and recent.
  • Too many lines destroy information; one level usually matters per chart.
  • Levels are zones a few pips deep; judge breaks on closes beyond the whole zone.
  • A top-down routine (daily, H4, H1, choose, delete) builds the map in minutes.
  • Always know the next higher-timeframe level beyond the break: it defines your room to run.

quiz.q: Why should a breakout level be obvious rather than hidden?
options: Brokers only fill orders at obvious levels
A breakout needs other traders' stops and entries beyond the level to carry it
Obvious levels never fail
Hidden levels are not allowed by most platforms
quiz.why: Breakouts run on the crowd's orders. A level nobody sees has no fuel behind it.

quiz.q: In 'A level is an area a few pips deep', why did the zone matter?
options: It made the chart look tidier
Wicks pierced the one-pip line, but no candle closed beyond the zone, so the level held
It showed the level was broken four times
It replaced the need for a stop-loss
quiz.why: Treated as a line, the level was 'broken' by wicks. Treated as a zone and judged on closes, it held every test.

quiz.q: You trade H1. Which pair of levels best follows the course's division of labour?
options: Use the H1 level for targets and the daily level for entries
Use the H1 level for entry timing and the daily level for direction and targets
Ignore daily levels completely
Only trade daily levels on the H1 chart
quiz.why: The higher timeframe governs direction and where to take profit; the execution timeframe governs when to act.

quiz.q: Your stop would be 20 pips and the next daily resistance is 25 pips beyond the breakout. What should you conclude?
options: Excellent trade: very close target
Barely 1.25R of room — the break runs straight into a wall; likely skip
Widen the stop to 40 pips
Ignore the daily level
quiz.why: Room to run measured in risk units is about 1.25R, below the illustrative 2R filter. Widening the stop makes it worse.

quiz.q: In the drill chart, why was the ceiling high-quality but not yet a trade?
options: It had only one touch
A level only becomes a trade after a candle closes clearly beyond it — and ideally retests
The daily level was too far away
H1 ceilings cannot be traded
quiz.why: Quality describes the level. The trade needs the break (a close beyond the zone) and, by this course's default, a holding retest.

lessons.title: Breakout Candle Quality
lessons.summary: Grade any breakout candle A, B or C from its close, body, size, wick and follow-through, and refuse the breaks that fail the grade.
lessons.module_title: Module 2 — The Break and the Entry
lessons.html:
You have found a level that matters and a consolidation that is genuinely coiled. Now price reaches the level and a candle pushes through. This is the moment most breakout traders make their worst decisions, because it is the moment of maximum adrenaline and minimum information.

The breakout candle carries more information than most traders read from it. Its close, its body, its size and its wicks tell you a good deal about who is pushing and how hard. The candles that follow tell you even more. This lesson turns that information into a simple grade — A, B or C — so the candle becomes data against a checklist instead of a starting gun.

The close is the vote that counts

Before anything else: a breakout is judged on the candle's close, on your chosen timeframe. Not on a tick through the level, not on the high of a candle that is still forming. Price can trade 20 pips beyond a level in the middle of an hour and close back inside it by the end. That candle did not break the level. It tested the orders above it and was rejected.

Waiting for the close costs you the first few pips of the genuine breaks. In exchange it removes a large share of the false ones — the wick-only "breaks" that are really rejections. On balance that is a trade worth making, and it is the first rule of this course.

The upper wick on that candle is a record of failure. Buyers pushed price through the level, the orders above it were filled, and sellers absorbed the lot and drove price back down before the hour ended. Anyone who bought on a stop order above the level was underwater before the candle had even closed.

KEY POINT

A wick beyond a level is a question. Only the close is an answer.

Five things to read in the breakout candle

1. Where it closed. Clearly beyond the whole level zone, not a pip or two through it. A close just inside the far edge of the zone is not a break; it is still a test.

2. Body size relative to its range. A strong breakout candle is mostly body. As a working guide, look for a body that is at least about 60% of the candle's total high-to-low range, with the close in the outer quarter of the candle — near the high for an upside break. That says buyers were in control from open to close, not just at one moment.

3. Size relative to recent candles. The candle should be noticeably larger than the candles inside the consolidation — roughly one and a half to two and a half times the recent average range is healthy. A breakout candle the same size as everything else shows no change in participation. A candle four or five times the average is a different problem, covered below.

4. The wick against the break. A long upper wick on an upside break means sellers were already pushing back before the close. A small one means they were not.

5. The approach. Was the break built — rising lows pressing into the level, pullbacks getting shallower — or launched in one vertical candle from the middle of the range? Built breaks have a crowd behind them. Launched ones often do not.

The candle that is too big

It seems logical that the bigger the breakout candle, the better. Up to a point it is. Beyond that point, size becomes a liability.

A candle four or five times the average range, closing far beyond the level, has three problems. First, it may be an exhaustion move: everyone who wanted to buy has bought in that one candle, leaving nobody for the follow-through. Second, it often prompts a deep retracement, because the market has travelled too far too fast. Third, and most practically, it wrecks your trade maths. If you buy at the close of a 60-pip candle and your logical stop sits back below the broken level, your stop is 60 pips wide. The same target that offered 3R from a sensible entry now offers 1R.

The answer to an oversized break is not to buy the close with a tight, arbitrary stop. That stop would sit in the middle of the candle, in the noise, and a normal retracement would take it out. The answer is either to skip, or to wait for the retest at the broken level — the subject of the next two lessons.

COMMON MISTAKE

Placing a tight stop under the close of a huge breakout candle to make the risk "fit". The stop is now in no-man's-land, and an ordinary pullback will hit it on the way to the retest.

Follow-through: the next one to three candles

The breakout candle is only half the evidence. The candles that follow ratify or veto it. After a genuine break, the market should show acceptance: price stays beyond the level, perhaps pauses or drifts, but does not slice back through. After a weak break, it sits there looking embarrassed: small candles, no progress, momentum leaking away.

Use a simple traffic-light rule for the one to three candles after the break:

  • Green: continuation, or a small pause that holds beyond the zone. The break is accepted.
  • Yellow: two or three candles of nothing, drifting back towards the zone. Downgrade the break; no new entries on momentum.
  • Red: a close back inside the range. The break has failed. Exit any position at once.

Putting it together: the A, B, C grade

Grade every breakout in writing, before you know the outcome.

  • A grade: decisive close clearly beyond the zone; body mostly body, close near the extreme; size about 1.5–2.5x the recent average; small wick against the break; a built approach; trend-aligned; room to run. Candidate for the momentum entry or the retest.
  • B grade: close beyond the zone and a reasonable body, but one lesser ingredient missing — an ordinary approach, a slightly oversized candle, or a modest wick. Retest entry only.
  • C grade: marginal close, small body, a large wick against the break, a launched approach, or an oversized exhaustion candle. No momentum entry. Many traders skip C-grade breaks entirely; at most, demand an exceptionally clean retest.

Not graded at all: a wick through the level with a close inside. That is not a breakout.

Going deeper

Measure, do not eyeball. For testing, make the grade mechanical. Define body ratio as |close − open| ÷ (high − low). Define relative size as the candle's range ÷ the average range of the previous 20 candles. Define clearance as the distance of the close beyond the zone edge, measured in ATR or in pips. Record these three numbers for every break in your journal alongside the outcome. After a hundred examples you will know which thresholds actually separate the breaks that hold from the ones that fail in your market, rather than relying on this lesson's starting points.

Timeframe of the close. A break that closes beyond the level on the H1 but is still a long-wicked candle on the H4 is weaker than it looks. If you trade H1 breaks of an H4 level, glance at the forming H4 candle. Conversely, waiting for an H4 close on an H1 setup usually costs too much: the retest has often come and gone.

Gaps and spikes. Around the weekly open and major data releases, prices can jump through a level with almost no trading in between. A "break" that happens in a gap has not been tested by orders at the level at all. Treat it as unconfirmed until price has traded and closed beyond the level in normal conditions. Lesson 9 covers news-driven breaks.

Body ratio can mislead on small candles. A tiny candle can be all body and still say nothing. That is why size relative to recent candles sits alongside the body ratio. You want both: a large candle that is mostly body.

Volume. Spot FX has no central volume, and broker tick volume is only a rough proxy for activity. If your platform shows tick volume, a breakout candle on clearly elevated tick volume is mildly supportive evidence. Do not build rules around it without testing, and never treat it as more important than the close and the follow-through.

THE RULES
  • Judge every break on a closed candle of your execution timeframe. No close beyond the zone, no break.
  • Grade the candle A, B or C in writing before you know the outcome.
  • No momentum entries on B or C grades; C grades need an exceptional retest or are skipped.
  • Never place an arbitrary tight stop inside a huge breakout candle to make the risk fit.
  • A close back inside the range after the break is an immediate exit.

Summary

  • The close on your timeframe is the vote that counts; a wick beyond the level is a rejection.
  • Read five things: close location, body ratio, size versus recent candles, opposing wick and the approach.
  • Oversized candles can be exhaustion and ruin your stop placement; prefer the retest or skip.
  • The next one to three candles ratify or veto the break: green, yellow or red.
  • Grade A, B or C before the outcome is known, and let the grade decide which entries are allowed.

quiz.q: A candle trades 18 pips above resistance mid-hour and closes 2 pips below the zone. What is it?
options: An A-grade breakout
A rejection: the close is inside, so it is not a break
A B-grade breakout
A retest
quiz.why: Only the close counts. A long upper wick with a close inside the zone shows the orders above were absorbed.

quiz.q: Which candle best fits an A-grade upside break?
options: A 5x-average candle closing 60 pips above the level
A candle about 2x average size, ~85% body, closing well clear of the zone with a small upper wick
A small doji closing 1 pip above the zone
A candle with a long upper wick closing just above the level
quiz.why: Healthy size, a dominant body, a clear close beyond the zone and little opposing wick. The 5x candle risks exhaustion and an unusable stop.

quiz.q: Why is a very large breakout candle a practical problem even if it keeps going?
options: Brokers reject orders after big candles
The logical stop back below the level is far away, shrinking the reward-to-risk
It always produces a double top
It cannot be retested
quiz.why: Buying the close of a 60-pip candle forces a 60-pip-plus stop to reach structural invalidation, which ruins the trade maths.

quiz.q: In 'No follow-through', what was the 'yellow card'?
options: The breakout candle itself
Four small candles going nowhere above the level
The close back inside the range
The range high zone
quiz.why: Stalling with no progress after a break is a warning; the close back inside that followed was the red card.

quiz.q: A break grades B: good close and body, but it was launched from mid-range in one candle. Which entry does the course allow?
options: Momentum entry at full size
Retest entry only
No entry ever
Buy the next candle's open with a tight stop
quiz.why: B grades are restricted to the retest entry; momentum entries are reserved for A grades in favourable conditions.

quiz.q: Why is broker tick volume only weak evidence in spot FX?
options: It is always zero
There is no central exchange volume, so tick volume is just a rough activity proxy
It only works on gold
It is illegal to use
quiz.why: Spot FX is decentralised; tick volume approximates activity at one broker. It may support, but should not override, the close and follow-through.

lessons.title: The Retest Entry vs the Momentum Entry
lessons.summary: Compare the two ways to enter a breakout on price, stop, risk-reward and trap exposure, and choose between them from written conditions rather than mood.
lessons.module_title: Module 2 — The Break and the Entry
lessons.html:
Watch two competent traders handle the same breakout and you will see two different jobs. The momentum trader enters as the level breaks — on the close of the breakout candle — accepting a worse price and more traps in exchange for never missing a runner. The retest trader lets the break go, sets an alert at the broken level, and acts only if price comes back to it and holds.

Both approaches are legitimate. Both can be tested. They simply distribute pain differently, and choosing between them is really choosing which kind of pain you handle best. This lesson sets out the trade-off honestly, shows where each entry fails, and gives you a way to choose that does not depend on how your last trade went.

Same break, two entries

The cleanest way to see the difference is on one chart. Here is a single breakout, entered two ways, with the same target.

The numbers are illustrative, but the shape of the comparison is general. The retest entry offers a better price, a tighter stop that sits at a logical place, and one extra layer of confirmation: the broken level has been tested and has held. In this example, the reward available per unit of risk roughly tripled.

What the retest costs you

If that were the whole story, nobody would ever take a momentum entry. Here is the rest of it: sometimes the retest never comes. And the breaks that do not retest are not a random sample. They are disproportionately the most urgent, most powerful moves — the ones driven by real, persistent demand.

That is the honest trade. Waiting for the retest costs you participation. In exchange you get price, a logical tight stop, a confirmation filter, and a calmer decision. A retest entry is a decision made while price is quiet at a level you chose in advance. A momentum entry is a decision made while a large candle is printing and every instinct says "go". Over hundreds of trades, the state you make decisions in is itself part of your edge.

What the momentum entry costs you

The momentum entry's failure mode is the trap from Lesson 1, taken at the worst price.

Look at how the retest filter worked here. A genuine retest is a controlled return to the level that holds. This was a violent candle straight through it. The retest trader had nothing to buy. The momentum trader was already in.

The momentum entry also has a stop problem. The logical invalidation point is back inside the range, often 30–50 pips from a breakout-close entry on H1. Traders who do not like that distance tend to use a tight, arbitrary stop instead — and arbitrary stops placed inside the noise are how momentum traders die of a thousand small cuts.

KEY POINT

The retest trades participation for confirmation. The momentum entry trades confirmation for participation. Neither is free; choose which cost you will pay, in advance.

Choose by conditions, not mood

The wrong way to choose is by recent memory: chasing breaks after watching one leave without you, then swearing off them after the next trap. That is the market managing you. The right way is to let written, observable conditions select the entry.

Momentum entries earn their place when urgency is likely: - An A-grade breakout candle (Lesson 4). - A break in the direction of a clear higher-timeframe trend. - A long, tight coil resolving — the tighter the spring, the less likely a polite pullback. - An active session (London or New York) with real participation.

Retest entries earn their place when scepticism is warranted: - B-grade candles, or any doubt about the grade. - Counter-trend breaks. - Breaks from loose or short consolidations. - Quiet or transitional sessions. - A level that has already produced one failed break.

For intermediate traders, this course takes a clear view: the retest is the default, and the momentum entry is the earned exception. Not because momentum entries are wrong, but because their failure mode — a run of chased breaks that instantly reverse — is expensive in the currency intermediate traders are shortest of: discipline. Missed trades cost pride. Trapped trades cost money and confidence.

Here is how that sounds as a written rule, by way of illustration: "EUR/USD and GBP/USD H1, trend-continuation breaks of a coil lasting 20+ bars, during London or New York: momentum tranche on an A-grade close plus retest tranche. Counter-trend breaks, B or C grades, and anything after 16:00 UK time: retest only. A level that has already failed once this week: retest only, with a confirmation candle." It takes two minutes to write and it removes the most expensive decision in breakout trading from the moment you are least able to make it.

Notice that the rule is about the setup, not about the trader's feelings. It does not say "momentum when confident". Confidence is not observable and it is at its highest straight after a winning streak — precisely when traders get careless.

The hybrid: splitting the position

Many experienced breakout traders refuse the either/or and split the risk.

As an illustration of the mechanics: a trader planning to risk 1% of the account on a setup might risk 0.5% on the confirmed break (wider stop, back inside the structure) and hold the other 0.5% for the retest (tighter stop). Because each half has a different stop distance, each half has its own position size; the risk in money is what is split, not the lot size. If the market runs without retesting, half is aboard. If the break fails outright, only half the risk was taken at the worst price.

The hybrid does not beat both pure approaches in every scenario — nothing does. Its value is psychological: it removes the agony of the all-or-nothing choice at the moment of the break, which is exactly when your judgement is worst.

COMMON MISTAKE

Deciding the entry style in the moment. In the moment, you will always choose whatever soothes the last loss. Write the rule per setup type before the session.

Going deeper

Thinking in expectancy, not win rate. The two entries produce different trade populations, so compare them on expectancy, not on how often they win. A purely hypothetical example: suppose a momentum approach takes 100 qualifying breaks, wins 45 at an average of 1.5R and loses 55 at 1R — expectancy (0.45 × 1.5) − 0.55 = +0.125R per trade, +12.5R in total. Suppose a retest approach on the same 100 breaks gets filled on only 55, wins 28 of them at an average of 3R and loses 27 at 1R — expectancy per trade (28 × 3 − 27) ÷ 55 ≈ +1.04R, about +57R in total. These numbers are invented to show the method. Your own tests may show something quite different, especially in strongly trending markets where the missed runners matter more.

The selection bias in missed trades. When you backtest the retest approach, the trades it misses are not random — they skew towards the strongest moves. A backtest that only measures filled trades will flatter the retest approach slightly in "average winner" terms and hide what it gave up. Always log the missed breaks and what they did, so you can see the opportunity cost.

Limit orders versus confirmation at the retest. Some retest traders place a limit order at the broken level and let price fill them. That captures more retests, including shallow ones, but it also fills you on the retests that fail. Others wait for a confirmation candle at the level — a pin bar, an engulfing, or simply a close back in the breakout direction. The confirmation approach gives up some fills and some price in exchange for fewer failed retests. The next lesson treats this in detail; test both.

Time stops on the retest. A retest that comes within roughly 3–15 candles of the break belongs to the same breakout. One that arrives two days later is a different market revisiting an old level. Many traders cancel the retest alert after a fixed number of candles or at the end of the session.

THE RULES
  • Decide the entry style per setup type in writing before the session, never in the moment.
  • Default to the retest entry. Momentum entries only on A-grade, trend-aligned breaks in an active session.
  • Momentum stops go where the idea dies (back inside the structure), never at an arbitrary tight distance.
  • In the hybrid, split the money at risk, not the lot size; size each half to its own stop.
  • No hold at the retest, no retest entry.

Summary

  • Momentum entries buy participation at the cost of price, stop distance and trap exposure.
  • Retest entries buy price, a logical stop and confirmation at the cost of missed runners — usually the strongest ones.
  • Choose by observable conditions: A-grade, trend-aligned, active-session breaks can justify momentum; everything else defaults to the retest.
  • The hybrid splits the money at risk between the break and the retest and softens the all-or-nothing decision.
  • Compare approaches on expectancy, and log the trades the retest approach misses.

quiz.q: In the two 'same break' charts, why did the retest entry offer roughly three times the reward-to-risk?
options: It used a bigger target
Its entry was closer to a logical stop, so risk per trade was far smaller for the same target
It used a bigger position
It ignored the stop
quiz.why: Same target, but a 16-pip stop instead of a 36-pip stop — the entry at the retest sat right next to its invalidation point.

quiz.q: What is the main, unavoidable cost of the retest approach?
options: Wider stops
Missing breaks that never return — often the strongest ones
More false breakouts
Higher spreads
quiz.why: Urgent breaks often do not retest, so the retest trader systematically misses some of the best moves.

quiz.q: In 'Where the momentum entry dies', why did the retest trader avoid the loss?
options: They used a smaller position
Price sliced back through the level instead of holding it, so there was no valid retest to buy
They entered short at the break
They used a wider stop
quiz.why: A valid retest is a controlled return that holds. A violent candle straight through the level is a failed break, not a retest.

quiz.q: Which conditions most justify a momentum entry under this course's rules?
options: A B-grade counter-trend break in the late Asian session
An A-grade break out of a tight coil, with the higher-timeframe trend, during London
Any break after three losing trades
A break of a level that already failed once
quiz.why: Momentum entries are reserved for A-grade, trend-aligned breaks in active sessions. The others call for the retest or no trade.

quiz.q: A trader running the hybrid plans 1% total risk. Half 1 has a 40-pip stop, half 2 a 15-pip stop. How should the positions be sized?
options: Same lot size for both halves
Each half risks 0.5% of the account, so half 2 uses a larger lot size than half 1
Half 1 risks 1%, half 2 risks 0%
Both use the 40-pip stop
quiz.why: The money at risk is split; each half's lot size is calculated from its own stop distance, so the tighter-stopped half carries more lots.

quiz.q: Why should you log breaks the retest approach missed when backtesting?
options: To increase the win rate
Because missed breaks skew towards the strongest moves, and ignoring them hides the method's opportunity cost
Because brokers require it
To calculate spread costs
quiz.why: Without the missed trades, a backtest flatters the retest approach and conceals what it gave up.

lessons.title: Role Reversal at the Retest
lessons.summary: Read whether a broken level has genuinely changed sides, and enter the retest only when the pullback, the reaction at the zone and the timing all agree.
lessons.module_title: Module 2 — The Break and the Entry
lessons.html:
After a genuine breakout, price very often does something that feels wrong to newer traders: it comes back. Having broken through resistance, the market pauses, rolls over and returns to the level it has just broken. The beginner sees failure. The experienced breakout trader sees the entry the whole strategy has been waiting for.

That return is the retest, and what you are looking for during it is role reversal: broken resistance behaving as support, or broken support behaving as resistance. When the level holds in its new role, you have confirmation that the break was real, an entry right next to a logical stop, and a clear line that tells you quickly if you are wrong. When it does not hold, you have avoided a failed breakout for the price of a missed entry.

This lesson teaches you to read that moment: why levels flip, what a healthy retest looks like, what a failing one looks like, and the exact evidence to demand before you enter.

Why a broken level changes sides

Levels have no magic. They flip because human decisions cluster around them. Three groups of traders do most of the work.

Trapped traders. Some traders sold the old resistance and did not exit when it broke. They are now underwater. When price returns to their entry, many close at breakeven with relief — and closing a short means buying. Their buying arrives exactly at the old level.

Latecomers. Traders who believed in the break but missed it, or refused to chase, now get a second chance at a better price. Their bids cluster at the level they watched break.

Adders. Larger participants who drove the break rarely fill everything in one push. A pullback to the broken level is a natural place to add.

None of this requires the level to be special in itself. It requires only that enough people saw it — which is why Lesson 3's obvious, tested levels produce the best retests.

What a healthy retest looks like

Judge every retest on three things, in this order.

1. The character of the pullback. You want a correction, not a collapse. A healthy pullback to the broken level drifts back on smaller candles, overlapping and mixed in colour, reluctant. It looks like profit-taking, not like sellers taking control. A pullback made of large, consecutive candles slamming back towards the level is a market that may be about to reject the break entirely.

2. Behaviour at the level. This is where the trade is decided, so demand evidence rather than assuming the level will hold. The classic signs: - A rejection wick into the zone with a close back outside it in the breakout direction — the pin bar. - An engulfing candle at the zone in the breakout direction. - At minimum, a candle that closes back away from the zone in the breakout direction after touching it.

Remember the level is a zone. Price may dip a few pips into it — even briefly through the far side of it — sweep the tightest stops, and hold. Judge the close, not the wick.

3. Time. Retests are freshest within a handful of candles of the break — as a working guide, roughly 3 to 15 candles on your execution timeframe. A "retest" two days later, after the chart has built new structure, is a different market revisiting an old level. It may be tradeable, but not on this playbook's terms.

KEY POINT

A retest is not a touch of the level. It is a touch of the level followed by evidence that the level is holding in its new role — and the evidence is a close.

The short side: broken support becomes resistance

Everything works in mirror image. When support breaks, a healthy retest drifts back up to the underside of the old floor and is rejected there.

When the retest fails

The retest improves the price you pay for uncertainty. It does not remove the uncertainty. Some retests that tick every box still fail, and you need to know what that looks like so you can take the loss without hesitation.

Could the failure have been spotted in advance? Partly. The pullback from the breakout high came back on larger candles than the healthy example earlier in this lesson, and it reached the level in fewer bars. That is a yellow flag, not a red one — plenty of retests with a slightly brisk pullback hold perfectly well. The point is not to find a reason after the event; it is to keep the loss at exactly the size you planned.

Notice how small and fast that loss was. The structure told you within three candles, cheaply, that the break had failed. Compare that with the momentum trader in Lesson 5, who lost from the top of the breakout candle. A failed retest is the method working, not failing. Confirmation was never a guarantee — it was a discount on the cost of being wrong.

COMMON MISTAKE

Moving the stop lower when the retest starts to fail, "because the level is a zone". The zone was already inside your stop. Once a candle closes through the whole zone, the role reversal has failed and so has the trade.

The entry, step by step

  1. After an A or B-grade break, set an alert at the outer edge of the broken zone.
  2. When the alert fires, check the character of the pullback: drifting and overlapping, or violent and one-sided? If violent, stand aside.
  3. At the zone, wait for a closed confirmation candle in the breakout direction: pin bar, engulfing, or a strong close away from the zone.
  4. Enter at that candle's close (or on a small limit just inside it).
  5. Stop beyond the confirmation candle's extreme and beyond the zone, plus a few pips for the spread.
  6. Target the next real level (Lesson 9 covers targets).
  7. Cancel the idea if no valid retest has formed within about 15 candles, or if any candle closes back through the whole zone.

Practice drill

Going deeper

Limit order or confirmation? Two schools exist. The limit-order trader rests a buy order at the outer edge of the zone and is filled on every touch, including shallow retests that never quite reach the middle of the zone and fast ones that never print a signal. The confirmation trader waits for a closed candle and gets fewer, later, slightly worse fills — but skips most of the retests that slice straight through. Neither is objectively better. Test both on the same set of breaks and compare expectancy, not win rate.

Depth of the retest. Retests do not always reach the level. In strong markets price may stop a few pips above the zone — a "shallow" or "near" retest — and never fill a trader waiting at the zone itself. Some traders accept a confirmation candle within a set distance of the zone, for example within about a quarter of the average candle range. Others treat a shallow hold as a reason to take a momentum-style entry with a structural stop. Decide in advance.

Second retests. Occasionally price retests, bounces, and returns to the level a second time. A second hold is often stronger evidence than the first, because sellers have had two chances and failed twice. A third return is a warning: the level is being worn away. Each extra visit uses up more of the buying that defended it.

Retest on a lower timeframe. Some traders identify the break on H1 and read the retest on M15 for a tighter confirmation and stop. This improves the reward-to-risk on paper but introduces more noise and more false signals. If you do it, keep the H1 zone as your invalidation: the M15 signal decides when to enter, the H1 zone decides whether you are still right.

Role reversal is not guaranteed by touch count. A level rejected five times before it broke has, in theory, more trapped traders to defend its retest. In practice, very heavily tested levels sometimes break with such force that no retest comes at all — the runner case from Lesson 5.

THE RULES
  • Enter a retest only after a closed confirmation candle at the zone in the breakout direction.
  • No entry if the pullback to the level is faster and stronger than the breakout leg.
  • Stop goes beyond the confirmation candle's extreme and beyond the zone, plus spread.
  • Any close through the whole zone ends the trade and the idea. Never widen the stop.
  • Cancel the retest idea after about 15 candles without a valid signal.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • The level was obvious and tested before the break
  • The breakout candle graded A or B
  • The pullback drifted back on smaller, overlapping candles
  • A closed confirmation candle (pin, engulfing or strong close) formed at the zone
  • The retest came within about 15 candles of the break
  • Stop placed beyond the signal candle and the zone, sized to 0.5–1% risk
  • At least 2R of room to the next higher-timeframe level

Summary

  • Broken levels flip because trapped traders exit, latecomers enter and larger players add — all at the same obvious price.
  • Judge a retest on the pullback's character, the evidence at the zone (a close) and the time since the break.
  • Mirror everything for shorts: broken support retested as resistance.
  • Failed retests produce small, fast losses; take them without moving the stop.
  • A violent return to the level is a failing break, not a retest.

quiz.q: Which group helps a broken resistance level act as support on the retest?
options: Traders who shorted the old resistance closing at breakeven, which means buying
Brokers adjusting spreads
Traders selling new shorts at the level
Central banks defending the level
quiz.why: Closing a short is a buy order, and trapped shorts tend to close near their entry — right at the old level.

quiz.q: In 'A healthy retest: drift, test, engulf', what was the entry signal?
options: The first touch of the zone
A bullish engulfing candle at the zone closing back above it
The breakout candle
A break of the range low
quiz.why: The trigger is a closed confirmation candle at the zone. A touch alone is not evidence that the level is holding.

quiz.q: In the drill, why was the return to the level not a retest to buy?
options: It came too late
It was three large, consecutive red candles — a collapse, with no confirmation at the zone
The breakout was A-grade
The level had too many touches
quiz.why: A pullback faster and stronger than the breakout leg signals sellers taking control, and no confirming close formed.

quiz.q: Your retest long is in place; a candle closes below the whole zone. What does the course say?
options: Widen the stop because the level is a zone
Exit: the role reversal has failed and the trade idea is dead
Add to the position at a better price
Wait for the next session
quiz.why: The zone was already accounted for inside the stop. A close through the whole zone invalidates the trade.

quiz.q: For a short on a retest of broken support, where does the stop go?
options: Below the entry
Above the confirmation candle's high and the zone, plus spread
At a fixed 10 pips
At the range high
quiz.why: Mirror of the long rule: beyond the signal candle's extreme and beyond the zone, with a spread buffer.

quiz.q: What is the honest cost of the confirmation approach compared with a resting limit order at the zone?
options: Larger losses on failed retests
Fewer and slightly later fills, missing some shallow or fast retests
It never misses a trade
It requires wider stops always
quiz.why: Waiting for a closed candle filters many failing retests but gives up some fills and some price.

lessons.title: False Breaks and Reclaims
lessons.summary: Recognise a false break as it happens, exit without negotiation, and — when the conditions qualify — trade the reclaim in the opposite direction.
lessons.html:
You will be caught by false breakouts. Everyone who trades this strategy is, regularly, for as long as they trade it. The aim is not to avoid them completely, which is impossible, but to be caught less often, to pay less each time, and — once you understand them well enough — to occasionally be on the right side of one.

That last point is the shift this lesson asks you to make. A false break is not just a failed trade. It is information. When a level breaks and price then reclaims it — closes back on the original side — the traders who bought the break are trapped, and their exits are about to push price the other way. A failed breakout is often a better trade than the breakout was.

The anatomy of a false break

A false break has three parts. Learn to see each one as it forms.

1. The poke. Price trades beyond an obvious level, triggering stop orders and breakout entries beyond it.

2. The absorption. The burst of buying (for an upside false break) is met by selling that soaks it up. The candle stalls, leaves a long wick beyond the level, or goes nowhere for a few bars.

3. The reclaim. A candle closes back inside the range — on the original side of the level. This is the moment the break is dead. Everyone who bought it is now underwater, and their stops sit inside the range below.

Fingerprints you can see in real time

Most false breaks are the mirror image of Lesson 4's checklist.

  • The wick without the close. Price trades through the level but the candle closes back inside. The most common false break, and the one closing-basis confirmation filters out entirely.
  • The close without follow-through. A candle does close beyond the level, but the next two or three go nowhere. Momentum bleeds away. Yellow card.
  • The re-entry. A candle closes back inside the range. Red card. The breakout idea is dead.

And the context tells, which you can check before the poke happens:

  • The break is against the higher-timeframe trend.
  • A bigger level sits just beyond the break.
  • The range was sloppy, not coiled.
  • The session is thin: late Asia, the hour after the London close, holiday periods.
  • The level has already produced one failed break recently, or is being tested for the fifth or sixth time with no compression.
KEY POINT

If you are in a breakout trade and a candle closes back inside the range, you exit. No waiting for the stop, no hoping. The first loss is the cheapest.

There is also a behavioural fingerprint, and it is in you. If you notice that you badly want to buy a breakout candle — that it feels urgent, that it is "leaving without you" — treat that feeling as a mild contrary indicator. False breaks work precisely because they produce that feeling in thousands of traders at once. Urgency is what the pool of breakout orders is made of. A written plan turns the feeling into a question you can answer calmly: has the candle closed, what grade is it, and what is the context?

A note on "liquidity sweeps"

Some frameworks, notably Smart Money Concepts, call this pattern a liquidity sweep or stop hunt and describe it as institutions deliberately running stops before reversing. Keep two things separate. What the chart observably shows is price trading beyond an obvious level, failing to hold, and closing back inside. What the framework calls it is a story about intent, which nobody outside those institutions can verify. You do not need the story to trade the pattern. Price first. Framework second.

Trading the reclaim

For some traders the failed break is the setup. The logic is straightforward: once price has reclaimed the level, the trapped breakout traders' stops sit inside the range in the direction you want to trade, and the far side of the range is a natural target.

The rules, for an upside false break (sell):

  1. Qualify the context. A clear range with defined boundaries; ideally the higher-timeframe trend is down or neutral, or a bigger level sits just above the poke.
  2. Wait for the reclaim close. A candle must close back inside the range, below the zone. Wicks back inside are not enough.
  3. Entry. At the close of the reclaim candle, or on a small pullback to the underside of the zone.
  4. Stop. Above the extreme of the false break — the highest wick of the poke — plus a few pips for the spread. That is the point where the false break has become a real one.
  5. Target. The middle of the range first; the opposite boundary as the main objective.

Notice the honest weakness here: the stop has to sit beyond the whole poke, which is often a long way from the reclaim close. In this example the trade offered only about 1R to the range low. Reclaim trades often look more attractive than they are, because the move afterwards is fast and dramatic. Measure the reward-to-risk before you enter, not after. A pullback entry to the underside of the zone after the reclaim can improve it considerably — at the cost of sometimes missing the move.

When the reclaim fails

Fading a failed break is still a trade against an obvious level that just broke. Sometimes the "false" break turns out to be a pause, and the real breakout resumes.

The lesson is context. This "false break" happened in an uptrend, from a range with rising lows — the most bullish structure in Lesson 2. Fading it meant betting against both the trend and the lean. When the reclaim pattern appears in that context, the better response is usually to step aside, or to wait and see whether the breakout re-establishes itself, which would offer a fresh retest entry on the long side.

COMMON MISTAKE

Becoming a reflexive fader after a run of trapped breakouts. Fading every break is just the mirror image of buying every break. The reclaim trade needs the same context filters as the breakout trade.

Reclaims from below

The same pattern appears at support. Price breaks below a floor, triggers the sell stops of longs and the entries of breakdown sellers, then closes back above. In an uptrend, this is often one of the cleaner setups on the chart.

Practice drill

Going deeper

How long a poke can last. Some false breaks reclaim on the next candle; others spend five or six candles beyond the level before collapsing back. The longer price spends beyond the level, the more traders accept the break as real and the more are trapped when it fails — but also the more likely it is that the break really was real. A practical rule: treat any close back inside within about five candles as a reclaim; beyond that, treat it as a new structure.

The second break. After a reclaim, price sometimes breaks the same level again a few hours later and this time holds. Traders who were trapped once often refuse the second break, which can make it unusually clean. This is one reason this course treats "a level that has already failed once" as retest only, not never.

Reclaims and the opposite boundary. A failed upside break that reclaims the range often runs straight through the range and breaks the other side, because trapped longs' stops sit below the range low too. That second break is a legitimate breakout in its own right, but it is usually extended by the time it happens; the retest is the place to act on it.

Measuring your own false-break rate. In your journal, record for every breakout you grade: whether it reclaimed within five candles, the session, the trend alignment and the grade. Within a few months you will know which combinations fail most often in the markets you trade, which is worth more than any general statistic.

THE RULES
  • In a breakout trade, any candle close back inside the range is an immediate exit.
  • A reclaim requires a candle close back inside; a wick back inside is not enough.
  • Fade a failed break only with supporting context: counter-trend break, bigger level overhead, or a sloppy range.
  • Never fade a break out of a coiled, trend-aligned structure with rising lows (or falling highs for shorts).
  • Reclaim stops go beyond the extreme of the false break plus spread; check the reward-to-risk before entry.

Summary

  • A false break has three parts: the poke, the absorption and the reclaim close.
  • Most false breaks show fingerprints beforehand: counter-trend, bigger level beyond, sloppy range, thin session.
  • Once a candle closes back inside the range, the break is dead — exit any breakout position.
  • The reclaim can itself be traded, with the stop beyond the poke and the range's far side as the target.
  • Reclaim trades need context; fading a coiled, trend-aligned break is the weakest version.

quiz.q: What exactly confirms a false break, under this course's rules?
options: A long wick beyond the level
A candle closing back inside the range
A stall of two candles
The price touching the far side of the range
quiz.why: The reclaim close is the confirmation. A wick or a stall is a warning, not proof.

quiz.q: Where does the stop go on a reclaim short after an upside false break?
options: Just above the reclaim candle's close
Above the extreme of the false break plus spread
At the range middle
Below the range low
quiz.why: The trade is wrong if price exceeds the poke's high — at that point the break has become real.

quiz.q: In 'A reclaim that fails', what made the short a weak trade?
options: The stop was too wide
It faded a break out of an uptrend with rising lows into the ceiling
The reclaim candle was too large
It was traded in London
quiz.why: Fading a coiled, trend-aligned structure bets against both trend and lean — the weakest context for a reclaim trade.

quiz.q: How should you describe a 'liquidity sweep' to keep it observable?
options: Banks deliberately hunting retail stops
Price traded beyond an obvious level, failed to hold and closed back inside
A secret institutional signal
A guaranteed reversal
