quiz.why: Describe what the chart shows; intent is the framework's story and cannot be verified. Price first. Framework second.

quiz.q: In the drill, why did the reclaim qualify as a short?
options: Because all false breaks should be faded
The upside break was counter-trend in a range below a falling 50 EMA, and a full-bodied candle closed back inside
Because the range was sloppy
Because the next candle was green
quiz.why: Both the pattern (close back inside) and the context (counter-trend break) supported the fade.

quiz.q: A reclaim trade offers 0.8R to the range low with the stop beyond the poke. What is a sensible response?
options: Take it with a tighter, arbitrary stop
Skip it, or wait for a pullback into the zone to improve the entry
Double the position size
Move the target beyond the range low without reason
quiz.why: Measure reward-to-risk before entry. A pullback entry can improve it; shrinking the stop arbitrarily puts it inside the noise.

lessons.title: Flags and Triangles as Breakout Structures
lessons.summary: Qualify flags, pennants and the three triangles by strict rules, trade their resolution with the break-and-retest method, and recognise when the pattern has expired.
lessons.html:
So far the consolidations in this course have been rectangles: a flat ceiling, a flat floor and price bouncing between them. Two other shapes deliver a large share of the cleanest breakouts in any market — flags (and their close relative, pennants) and triangles. They are not different strategies. They are the same compression-and-release story with a shape that tells you a little more about who is in control.

This lesson gives you strict rules for each, because the most common error with chart patterns is not trading them badly. It is seeing them where they do not exist.

Flags: the pole is the evidence

A flag has two parts, and the first matters more.

The pole is a sharp, impulsive move: large candles, mostly one colour, little overlap. It is the evidence that someone wanted in — or out — urgently. Without a genuine pole there is no flag, however neat the consolidation looks.

The flag is the rest that follows: a short, shallow, tidy drift against the pole's direction (a bull flag drifts down or sideways; a bear flag drifts up or sideways). It is early buyers taking profit, absorbed by latecomers glad of any pullback. Volatility drops visibly — small bodies, overlapping candles, boredom.

A pennant is the same event with a different rest: instead of a parallel channel, the pause contracts into a small symmetrical triangle. Trade it exactly like a flag.

Qualifying rules for flags

  1. An impulsive pole. Grade the pole first. Strong bodies, a clear streak, ideally breaking a prior level on the way. If the pole is a grind, stop reading.
  2. Shallow. A healthy flag usually holds the upper half of the pole — as a working guide, it retraces no more than about 50%. The deeper it cuts, the weaker the case.
  3. Counter-drift or sideways. A bull "flag" that keeps rising steeply is not resting; it is just trend, and rising consolidations after a pole often behave like wedges and break the other way.
  4. Brief. Flags are short relative to their pole — often one to three times the pole's duration. The longer the rest drags on, the more it becomes an ordinary range and the less the pole's urgency still means.
  5. Structure intact. If the flag breaks the last meaningful higher low (for a bull flag), the label is revoked on the spot.
KEY POINT

No pole, no flag. The pole is the evidence of urgency; the flag is just the pause that lets you join it.

When a "flag" is not a flag

Here is the version that catches traders who skip rule 2.

The honest diagnosis here is that the trader graded the break and forgot to grade the pattern. The breakout candle itself was respectable. But a pattern is a chain of evidence, and the chain had already snapped twice before the break arrived: the rest was deep, and it was long. By the time of the break, the pole's urgency was ancient history. A flag that takes longer than its pole and gives back more than half of it is simply a range that started after a rally — and it deserves range rules, not flag rules.

Triangles: three shapes, three stories

A triangle is a consolidation whose boundaries converge. Each type tells a slightly different story about who is losing patience.

Ascending triangle — flat top, rising lows. Sellers are defending a fixed price while buyers step in earlier and higher each time. Each test of the ceiling eats a little more of the resting supply. It leans bullish.

Descending triangle — flat floor, falling highs. The mirror image. Buyers defend a fixed price while sellers press lower highs into it. It leans bearish.

Symmetrical triangle — lower highs and higher lows. Both sides are getting more aggressive and neither has the upper hand. It is the most neutral of the three: usually a continuation of the prior trend, but with the least directional information.

"Lean" is doing careful work in those sentences. Ascending triangles break down and descending triangles break up often enough to keep everyone humble. The lean adjusts how much evidence you demand; it never replaces the break.

Qualifying rules for triangles

  1. At least two touches on each boundary, and preferably three on at least one. Two lines through two points each is geometry, not evidence.
  2. Genuine convergence. The swings must be shrinking. If they are not, you have a range or a channel.
  3. A prior move. A triangle within a trend is a continuation candidate; one after nothing in particular is chop.
  4. Volatility contracting towards the apex: smaller candles, smaller swings.
  5. For ascending and descending triangles, the flat side is the meaningful boundary. A break of the sloped side is softer information.

Let the market vote on symmetricals

With a symmetrical triangle, do not predict the direction. Mark both boundaries and trade the break that actually happens — with extra respect when it agrees with the prior trend, and extra suspicion (smaller size, retest only) when it does not.

The apex is a deadline

Two practical points that textbooks underplay.

First, breaks from roughly the middle two-thirds to three-quarters of a triangle's length tend to have the most conviction. A market that drifts all the way into the apex has usually let the tension leak away. What follows is more often a dribble — or a false break in both directions — than a clean expansion. If price reaches the tip with no resolution, downgrade the whole structure.

Second, triangles are false-break heaven. Everyone can see the same lines. A brief poke through one boundary that immediately reverses — a "throw-over" — is common. Everything from Lesson 7 applies: demand the close, watch the follow-through, respect a reclaim.

A useful habit is to measure the triangle's length from its first touch to the point where the two lines would meet, and mark the 75% point on the chart in advance. If no decisive close has come by then, you downgrade the structure before the late break tempts you — a decision taken calmly, hours earlier, rather than in the moment.

COMMON MISTAKE

Trading inside a triangle. The inside is a shrinking, whippy no-man's-land where both sides get stopped. The trade is the resolution, not the coil.

Practice drill

Going deeper

Measured moves, honestly. The classical objectives are the flag's pole projected from the breakout point, and a triangle's height at its widest projected from the break. They are estimating tools, not forecasts. Their real value is to force a question before entry: is there room for a move of this size before the next real level? If the measured move runs straight through a daily level, the level wins. Lesson 9 covers targets in full.

Wedges are not triangles. A rising wedge — both boundaries sloping upward, converging — looks superficially like a bull flag or an ascending triangle, but its usual resolution is downward, because each push higher achieves less. If both lines slope the same way and converge, treat it as a wedge and do not assume continuation.

Pattern stops. For a flag, the stop goes beyond the far side of the flag (below the flag low for a bull flag). For a triangle breakout entry, use the most recent swing inside the triangle rather than the far side of the whole pattern, which is usually too distant to size sensibly. For any retest entry, the retest rules from Lesson 6 apply.

Flags on the higher timeframe. A bull flag on the daily chart often appears as a multi-day range on H1. Recognising the larger pattern gives the H1 range breakout a measured objective and a reason to prefer the upside break.

Failure is information. A bull flag that breaks its low, or an ascending triangle that breaks its flat-side counterpart downward, has told you the buyers' story was wrong. Those failures often produce sharp moves for the reasons in Lesson 7 — trapped pattern traders exiting together.

THE RULES
  • No pole, no flag. Grade the pole before the flag.
  • A flag deeper than about half the pole, or longer than about three times the pole's duration, is not a flag.
  • Triangles need two or more touches on each line and visibly shrinking swings.
  • Do not trade inside a triangle; trade the confirmed close beyond a boundary.
  • Downgrade or skip breaks that occur at the apex.
  • Treat measured moves as estimates; the next real level overrides the arithmetic.

Summary

  • Flags and pennants are a pole followed by a shallow, brief, contracting rest; the pole is the evidence.
  • Triangles come in three types: ascending (bullish lean), descending (bearish lean) and symmetrical (neutral).
  • Trade the resolution with the same tools as any breakout: candle grade, retest, role reversal.
  • The apex is a deadline; breaks at the tip are weak and often false.
  • Measured moves estimate room to run; the level map has the final say.

quiz.q: What is the single most important feature that qualifies a flag?
options: A perfectly parallel channel
A genuine impulsive pole before the consolidation
At least ten candles in the flag
A moving average crossover
quiz.why: No pole, no flag. The pole is the evidence of urgency the pattern depends on.

quiz.q: In 'Not a flag', which rules had the pattern already failed before its break?
options: Pole and structure
Shallow and brief — it gave back ~60% of the pole over 36 candles
Triangle touch count
None — it was a valid flag
quiz.why: A rest that retraces most of the pole and drags on for a long time is a range, not a flag.

quiz.q: Which boundary matters most in an ascending triangle?
options: The rising lower line
The flat top
Both equally
Neither — only the apex
quiz.why: The flat side is where the defended supply sits; its break is the meaningful event.

quiz.q: How should you treat a symmetrical triangle's direction?
options: Predict it from the last candle
Let the market vote: trade the break that happens, with more respect for trend-aligned breaks
Always buy it
Always sell it
quiz.why: Symmetricals carry the least directional information. Trade the confirmed break, demanding more evidence when it fights the prior trend.

quiz.q: In the apex drill, why was the break a no-trade?
options: It closed too far beyond the line
It came at the very tip, as a marginal C-grade close with no meaningful stop
The triangle had too few touches
It was in the wrong session
quiz.why: Apex breaks have usually leaked their energy, and the converged lines leave no sensible invalidation point.

quiz.q: A bull flag's measured move projects 120 pips, but a daily resistance sits 70 pips above the break. What should the target be?
options: 120 pips — the pattern says so
Just before the daily resistance, about 70 pips
Double the measured move
No target; hold for ever
quiz.why: Measured moves are estimates. A real higher-timeframe level overrides the arithmetic.

lessons.title: Stops, Targets and News-Driven Breaks
lessons.summary: Place breakout stops where the idea dies, set targets from the level map and measured moves, manage the winner, and handle breaks caused by scheduled news.
lessons.module_title: Module 4 — Managing and Completing the Trade
lessons.html:
A good entry is worth nothing if the stop sits in the wrong place, and a good stop is wasted if the target asks the market for more than it can give. This lesson finishes the trade: where the stop goes and why, how far the target should be, how to manage a position that is working, and what to do when a level breaks because a data release has just hit the screen.

The stop goes where the idea dies

Every stop question starts in the same place: at what price is my trade idea provably wrong? Not "how much am I willing to lose" — that is decided by position size, a separate lever. The breakout idea is that a level has broken and will now hold in its new role. That idea dies when price re-establishes itself on the wrong side of the level.

For a retest entry, that gives a tight, logical stop: - beyond the extreme of the confirmation candle (the pin bar's wick, the engulfing candle's low); - beyond the far edge of the broken zone; - plus a buffer for spread and noise — a few pips on majors, more on gold or during wide-spread hours.

For a momentum entry, the idea dies back inside the structure: below the last higher low inside the range or flag for a long. That is further away, which is the momentum entry's built-in cost.

KEY POINT

Stop distance is decided by structure. Risk is decided by position size. Never move the stop to make the size feel better.

Sizing the position

Once the structural stop is set, the position size follows from your risk per trade. As an illustration: a £10,000 account risking 1% has £100 at risk. With a 20-pip stop on EUR/USD, where a standard lot is worth about $10 per pip (convert to your account currency), the position is roughly £100 ÷ 20 pips = £5 per pip. With a 40-pip stop, the same £100 buys £2.50 per pip. The money at risk is identical; only the size changes. Many traders use 0.5–1% per trade while learning a new setup; the figures here are illustrative, not a recommendation.

Targets: the level map first, the measured move second

A target answers one question: where is the next place the market is likely to stop? Two tools answer it, and they should agree.

The level map. The next real higher-timeframe level beyond the break — a daily swing high, a multi-day range boundary, a weekly level. You marked it in Lesson 3. This is your primary target, because it is where real orders sit.

The measured move. For a range, project the range's height from the breakout point. For a flag, project the pole. For a triangle, project its widest height. These are estimating tools. Their main job is to check that a move of normal size has room to happen before it hits the next wall.

When they disagree, the level wins. If the measured move projects 80 pips but a daily level sits 55 pips away, the honest target is just in front of the daily level.

Minimum reward-to-risk. Before entry, divide the distance to your target by your stop distance. Many traders require at least 2R to the first real level as a filter for this setup. Treat that as a starting point to test, not a law. If the trade cannot offer it, it is not a trade at this level.

Managing the winner

Breakout trades tend to resolve quickly in one direction or the other, which makes management simpler than for most setups. A clear, pre-written plan beats improvisation:

  1. Leave it alone until price has moved about 1R in your favour. Early stop-tightening is the most common way to turn good breakout trades into scratch trades.
  2. Optional partial. Some traders take a part (for example, a third to a half) off at 1–1.5R. It reduces variance; it also reduces expectancy if your winners regularly reach the full target. Test both.
  3. Trail behind structure, not by a fixed number of pips. For a long, move the stop to just below each new confirmed higher low on your execution timeframe.
  4. Exit on a reclaim. If price ever closes back inside the original range, the breakout idea is dead even if your stop has not been hit.
  5. At the target, take it. The target was set at a real level for a reason. Hoping for the measured move beyond a daily wall is how winners become breakevens.

News-driven breaks

Scheduled news — central bank decisions, inflation figures, US non-farm payrolls — produces the most dramatic breakouts on the calendar and some of the least reliable ones in the first minutes. Three things change around a release:

  • Spreads widen and liquidity thins in the seconds around the number, so fills can be far from the price you expected.
  • Price can gap through a level with almost no trading in between. A break that happened in a gap has not been tested by orders at the level at all.
  • The first move is often reversed. The initial spike reflects the headline; the following minutes reflect the detail, revisions and positioning. Spikes through a level that reverse within the hour are common.

Rules for news

  1. Know the calendar. Before each session, note tier-one releases for both currencies in the pair.
  2. No new breakout entries in the minutes before a tier-one release — as a working rule, from about 15 minutes before until at least the first execution-timeframe candle after it has closed.
  3. An existing position into news is a decision, not an accident. Either reduce it, move the stop to a level you can accept being gapped through, or close it. Remember that stops can be filled beyond their level in a gap.
  4. Judge the post-news break on the same rules as any other. After the release candle closes and spreads return to normal, a level that has broken and then holds on a retest is a genuine break. News often supplies the catalyst for a real expansion — the retest is how you tell which.

Practice drill

Going deeper

Buffers in volatility units. A fixed 3-pip buffer is fine on EUR/USD in London, too tight on GBP/JPY, and meaningless on gold. A more portable rule is a buffer of about 0.1–0.25 × ATR(14) of your execution timeframe beyond the structural point. Test the multiple; record how often stops are hit by less than the buffer.

Time stops. Breakouts that are working usually work quickly. If a retest entry has gone nowhere after, say, 10–15 candles — neither towards the target nor the stop — the expansion thesis is weakening. Some traders exit or reduce at that point. This is worth testing on your data rather than adopting on faith.

Expectancy and partials. Partial profits change the shape of your returns. Hypothetically: a strategy whose winners reach 3R half the time and 1R the other half has an average winner of 2R. Taking half off at 1R on every trade caps half the position at 1R, so the average winner falls to 1.5R — while the win rate rises slightly, because some trades that would have reversed to the stop now bank something. Whether that trade-off helps depends entirely on your data. Measure it.

Correlated breakouts. On a big US data day, EUR/USD, GBP/USD and gold may all break at once. Three breakouts at 1% risk each on the same USD story is one 3% bet. Cap total risk per theme.

Weekend and holiday gaps. A position held over the weekend can open beyond its stop. Breakout traders on H1–H4 generally either flatten before the Friday close or reduce size and accept the gap risk knowingly.

THE RULES
  • Stops go beyond the confirmation candle's extreme and the zone, plus a spread or ATR buffer — never inside the zone.
  • Position size is calculated from the stop distance and a fixed risk per trade (0.5–1% illustrative).
  • The target is the next real higher-timeframe level; measured moves only confirm there is room.
  • Require about 2R of room to the first real level before entering.
  • No new breakout entries from about 15 minutes before a tier-one release until the first post-release candle has closed.
  • Trail only behind confirmed structure; exit on any close back inside the original range.

Summary

  • The stop sits where the breakout idea dies: beyond the retest's extreme and the zone, with a buffer.
  • Size the position from the stop; never move the stop to fit a preferred size.
  • Targets come from the level map; measured moves check room to run, and the level wins when they disagree.
  • Manage winners with a written plan: patience to 1R, optional partials, trail behind structure.
  • News breaks spike, gap and often reverse; wait for the dust to settle and trade the retest.

lessons.summary: Run the whole strategy from level map to exit as a written, step-by-step playbook, and review three full worked trades — including a loser — against it.
lessons.module_title: Module 4 — Managing and Completing the Trade
lessons.html:
Everything in this course now fits on a single page. This capstone assembles it into a playbook you can run before and during every session, then walks through three complete trades from first glance to final exit: two winners and one loser. The loser matters most. A playbook is not proven by its winners; it is proven by whether its losers were small, planned and taken without argument.

A reminder before we start: every chart here is a training chart, illustrative rather than real market data, and nothing in this lesson is a signal or a recommendation. The aim is to show the process working, not to suggest any particular result.

The playbook, step by step

Before the session (five minutes)

  1. Calendar. Note tier-one releases for both currencies in each pair you watch. Mark the no-entry windows.
  2. Level map. Daily, then H4, then H1. Mark five or six levels per pair. Delete stale lines.
  3. Choose the level. For each pair, identify at most one level whose break you would trade. Note the next higher-timeframe level beyond it and the room to run.
  4. Grade the consolidation. Defined boundaries (two or more touches each side), meaningful duration, contraction, and context (trend-aligned or counter-trend). If it is noise, cross the pair off.
  5. Write the plan. Direction allowed, entry style (retest by default; momentum tranche only for A-grade, trend-aligned breaks in an active session), where the stop would go, and the target.

At the break

  1. Wait for the close. No close beyond the whole zone, no break.
  2. Grade the candle A, B or C: close location, body ratio, size versus recent candles, opposing wick, approach. Write the grade down.
  3. Watch the follow-through. Green, yellow or red. A close back inside the range ends the idea.

At the retest

  1. Alert at the zone. Judge the pullback's character: a drift is good; a collapse is a no-trade.
  2. Demand a closed confirmation candle at the zone: pin bar, engulfing, or a strong close away from the zone.
  3. Enter at that close. Stop beyond the confirmation candle's extreme and the zone, plus a buffer. Size to 0.5–1% risk (illustrative).
  4. Check the maths. At least about 2R of room to the target in front of the next real level. If not, no trade.

In the trade

  1. Leave it alone until about 1R. Optional partial at 1–1.5R if your testing supports it.
  2. Trail behind confirmed structure. Exit at once on any close back inside the original range.
  3. Take the target at the level. Journal the trade with its grade, entry style, session and outcome.

Worked trade 1: a range coil in an uptrend (win)

The plan. EUR/USD was in an H1 and daily uptrend, trading above a rising 50 EMA. For two days it had ranged beneath a ceiling at roughly 1.0894–1.0902, with five rejections and steadily rising lows: a coiled structure with a bullish lean. The next daily resistance sat about 76 pips above the ceiling. The written plan: longs only; retest entry by default; momentum tranche permitted if the break was A-grade in London.

The break. Early in London, a candle closed 18 pips above the zone, about 90% body, roughly twice the average range of the consolidation, with almost no upper wick, after a built approach. Grade A. This trader chose to run the retest-only version on this occasion and simply set an alert at the top of the zone.

The retest. Price drifted back over ten candles on small, mixed bodies — a correction, not a collapse. At the zone a pin bar wicked to 47 and closed at 60, back above the zone.

Execution. Entry at 60. Stop at 41: below the wick, below the zone, plus 3 pips. Risk 19 pips, sized to 1% of the account (illustrative). Target 122, in front of the daily level, giving about 3.3R. The trade was left alone until 1R, then trailed under new higher lows, and reached the target 15 candles later.

Review. Every rule followed. The win is not the point; the rules are.

Worked trade 2: a descending triangle on gold (win, short)

The plan. Gold was below a falling 50 EMA on H4, with a descending triangle: a flat floor tested five times and lower highs pressing down into it. Bearish lean, trend-aligned. The next H4/daily support sat roughly $10 below the floor. Plan: shorts only, retest entry.

The break. An H4 candle closed about $2.50 below the zone — a full body, about 1.5× average size, built approach. Grade A-minus: fine, retest only per the plan.

The retest. Eleven candles later, price drifted back up to the underside of the old floor. A bearish pin bar wicked into the zone and closed at −11, back below it.

Execution. Short at −11. Stop at +16: above the pin's wick and the zone, with a buffer suited to gold's wider spread. Target −88, in front of the next support: about 2.9R. Reached within ten candles.

Review. Rules followed. The buffer used was larger in pips than on EUR/USD because gold's spread and noise are larger — which is exactly why buffers should be expressed in volatility terms.

Worked trade 3: the retest that failed (loss)

The plan. USD/JPY on H1 had ranged for two days under a well-tested ceiling, in a neutral-to-mildly-bullish daily context, with about 60 pips of room to the next daily level. Plan: retest entry only.

The break. A candle closed 10 pips above the zone but with an upper wick a third of its range. Grade B. Momentum entry ruled out by the plan.

The retest. Price drifted back over ten candles — though somewhat brisker than ideal — and printed a bullish engulfing at the zone that closed at 58, back above it. Every rule satisfied.

Execution. Entry 58, stop 39 below the engulfing low and the zone plus buffer: 19 pips, 1% risk (illustrative). Target 104 in front of the daily level: about 2.4R.

What happened. Two candles later a full-bodied red candle closed through the whole zone. The stop was hit for −1R. The range low followed.

Review. Were the rules followed? Yes. Was the loss the planned size? Yes. Was there an earlier warning? The B grade and the slightly brisk pullback were both yellow flags, already priced in by restricting the trade to a retest entry. The correct response is to log it and take the next valid setup at the same size. Changing the rules after one loss would mean letting a single outcome rewrite a process that was built on many.

KEY POINT

A good trade is one that followed the plan. A winning trade is just one outcome. Judge yourself on the first; the market decides the second.

Practice drill

The strategy passport
Market Major FX pairs and gold, H1–H4, London and New York hours, with a clear higher-timeframe bias
Wait for A coiled consolidation (2+ touches each side, contracting) under or above an obvious, recent level with at least 2R of room beyond
Trigger A close clearly beyond the zone (grade A or B), then a retest holding the broken level with a closed pin bar, engulfing or strong close. Momentum tranche only on A-grade, trend-aligned breaks in an active session
Stop Beyond the confirmation candle's extreme and the zone, plus a spread/ATR buffer; size to 0.5–1% risk (illustrative)
Target In front of the next real higher-timeframe level, cross-checked with the measured move
Avoid Wick-only breaks, C grades, sloppy ranges, breaks into nearby walls, apex breaks, dead sessions, tier-one news windows, and any break that closes back inside

Going deeper: testing the playbook

A playbook is a hypothesis until you have tested it. A practical sequence:

  1. Historical review. Scroll back through at least 100 qualifying breaks on your chosen pairs and timeframe. For each, record the level quality, candle grade, entry style, session, trend alignment and the outcome in R — including the breaks that never retested.
  2. Split the results. Compare trend-aligned with counter-trend, A with B grades, London with New York, retest with momentum. The differences tell you which filters earn their place.
  3. Demo forward test. Trade the written rules on demo for at least a month, or 30–50 trades, without changing them. You are testing your execution as much as the rules.
  4. Review monthly. Change one rule at a time, and only when the data — not the last loss — says so.

The numbers you collect are the only ones that matter. This course has deliberately not quoted win rates, because they depend on market, timeframe, session and the exact definitions you use. Yours will be specific to you, and that makes them more useful than any general figure.

THE RULES
  • Write the plan before the session: level, allowed direction, entry style, stop location, target.
  • Only a close beyond the whole zone is a break; grade it A, B or C in writing.
  • Default to the retest; momentum entries only for A-grade, trend-aligned, active-session breaks.
  • Stop beyond the confirmation candle and the zone plus buffer; risk a fixed 0.5–1% (illustrative).
  • No trade without about 2R of room to the next real level.
  • Exit on any close back inside the original range. Never widen a stop.
  • No new entries in tier-one news windows.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Calendar checked; no tier-one release within the entry window
  • Level is obvious, tested (2+ touches) and recent; drawn as a zone
  • Consolidation is coiled, with defined boundaries and contraction
  • Higher-timeframe direction noted; trade direction allowed by the plan
  • Breakout candle closed clearly beyond the zone and graded A or B in writing
  • Follow-through was green or a calm pause — no close back inside
  • Pullback to the zone was a drift, not a collapse
  • Closed confirmation candle at the zone (pin bar, engulfing or strong close)
  • Stop beyond the signal candle and the zone, plus buffer
  • Position sized to a fixed 0.5–1% risk (illustrative)
  • At least about 2R of room to the target in front of the next real level
  • Exit plan written: trail behind structure, exit on reclaim, take the target

Summary

  • The playbook runs in four stages: before the session, at the break, at the retest, in the trade.
  • Worked trades 1 and 2 show the full process on a range and a triangle; trade 3 shows a valid trade losing exactly 1R.
  • The level map can veto a perfect pattern, as the drill showed.
  • The passport and checklist compress the whole course onto one page.
  • Test the playbook on at least 100 historical breaks and a demo period before trusting it.
